title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 127 (Punishment for failure to distribute dividends)

content.overview: Section 127 punishes a failure to pay a declared dividend, or to post the warrant, within thirty days. The company and every director who is knowingly a party to the default are liable. The section lists exceptions, including a legal bar, a disputed right, a lawful set-off, and a direction that the company cannot comply with.
content.glance: Dividend must be paid, or the warrant posted, within thirty days of declaration, failing which directors face the consequences in the section, subject to its exceptions.
content.study:
## Statutory rule
Section 127 provides that where a dividend has been declared by a company but has not been paid, or the warrant in respect thereof has not been posted, within thirty days from the date of declaration, every director who is knowingly a party to the default shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years and with fine which shall not be less than one thousand rupees for every day during which such default continues, and the company shall be liable to pay simple interest at the rate of eighteen per cent a year during the period for which such default continues.

The proviso lists exceptions, including where the dividend could not be paid by reason of the operation of any law, where a shareholder has given directions which cannot be complied with, where there is a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend, where the dividend has been lawfully adjusted against any sum due, and where the failure is not due to any default on the part of the company.

## Answer structure
State the thirty-day default, then check the proviso before imposing the penalty. Not a verified closure.

sections.heading: Rule
sections.body: Dividend must be paid, or the warrant posted, within thirty days of declaration, failing which directors face the consequences in the section, subject to its exceptions.

sections.heading: Explanation
sections.body: Exceptions include a dispute as to title, a lawful direction restraining payment, and a failure not due to any default of the company. The section does not authorise withholding a declared dividend for cash-flow convenience. Declaration itself is section 123.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.
